assessment.nobel_worthiness: An optical lattice clock combines the magic-wavelength lattice idea with narrow optical transitions in many atoms probed at once, taking fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and below. It is exactly the kind of measurement advance that opens new observation regimes: relativistic geodesy at centimetre height resolution, tests of constancy of fundamental constants, searches for dark-matter signatures, and a route to redefining the second. Originality and clarity of the central invention are high.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept (c. 2001-2003) and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye's group drove the record stability and accuracy, the Sr clock comparisons and the many-body/spin-exchange understanding. Two laureates form a clean and fair configuration. Other groups (Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Sterr, NIST, PTB) contributed important implementations, so the line has to be drawn around the invention and its leading realisation.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent clocks in several countries with agreed international comparisons. The redefinition of the second has not happened yet, but the technology is clearly mature and the recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views the Hall/Hänsch 2005 frequency-comb prize and the Wineland ion-clock work as already covering this area.
Credit to Lemonde, Gill, Ludlow, Sterr and others for competing lattice clock realisations and the ion-clock lineage may be raised.
The redefinition of the SI second is still pending.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 Cirac-Zoller proposal made controlled-NOT gates with trapped ions a concrete experimental programme; ion traps have since become one of the leading platforms for quantum computing and simulation, with high-fidelity gates, entanglement of many ions and error-corrected logical operations. It is a field-opening combination of theory and experiment, in which my own experimental instincts say that coherence times, gate fidelities and scalability were demonstrated rather than merely asserted.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller supplied the proposal; Blatt's group carried out the first Cirac-Zoller gate and the long run of benchmark experiments (entanglement of up to tens of ions, teleportation, quantum algorithms). Wineland (already awarded 2012) and Monroe, Wineland's group and the NIST/Innsbruck rivalry make the experimental credit complex. The three-person configuration is plausible but Monroe/Wineland-lineage credit is not supplied in the names.
assessment.maturity: Over 30 years of experimental validation by multiple groups and companies. Recognition is not premature, though it overlaps with the 2012 prize and with the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize in the broader quantum-computing area.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2012 Wineland/Haroche prize may reduce the appetite for a further ion-trap prize.
Experimental credit for the first gates is shared with the Boulder/NIST lineage, who are not among the supplied names.
Whether a quantum-computing prize should wait for a clear practical advantage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED places a superconducting qubit in a microwave resonator, gives strong coupling, dispersive readout and a bus for qubit-qubit interaction, and is the architecture used in nearly every superconducting quantum processor. The impact on the quantum technology field is large, and the experimental demonstration of strong coupling (2004) was a clean, reproducible measurement result.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote the 2004 theory proposal and the Wallraff et al. Nature paper demonstrated it. Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are a reasonable triplet, but Girvin and Huang are not in the supplied credit and the Yale team's wider credit is real.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups and used in commercial devices. The 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits touches adjacent ground, so the committee may feel the area has been recognised for now.
uncertainties: Possible reluctance after the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize.
Credit omission of Steven Girvin and other Yale co-authors, which the supplied names cannot repair.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms gives inertial sensors, gravimeters, gradiometers and tests of the equivalence principle and of the fine-structure constant at extremely high precision. This is a measurement technique that has opened new regimes, in line with my view that progress is limited by what can be measured, with applications in geodesy, navigation and fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated atom interferometry with a nanofabricated grating and later precision measurements; Bordé gave the theoretical framework for Ramsey-Bordé interferometry; Kasevich (with Chu) demonstrated the atom-interferometer gravimeter and gyroscope. Steven Chu was already awarded in 1997 for cooling and is not in the list; Chu, Ramsey and Bordé credit overlap, and Ramsey and Hänsch earlier prizes also touch the neighbourhood. Attribution is difficult to separate.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the laboratory with independent groups worldwide; field use and gravitational-wave-detector ambitions are still developing, so recognition is plausible but the biggest applications are not yet fully delivered.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 laser-cooling prize and Ramsey's 1989 separated-oscillatory-fields prize.
Fair split between Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and Chu is disputed, and Chu is not in the credited names.
Fundamental-physics results (e.g. equivalence-principle tests) have not yet exceeded classical limits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and quantum teleportation are two of the foundational protocols of quantum information; QKD is already in field deployment, and teleportation underlies quantum networking and repeaters. The concepts are original and conceptually clear, and have shaped an entire field of experimental work, including the quantum memories and repeaters I know from my own research.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard are the clear core pair for BB84 and the teleportation proposal; Ekert (E91) is a distinct and separate contribution that would make three, and Wootters/Zurek/Wiesner (no-cloning, conjugate coding) are not among the names. I would propose two, leaving Ekert out to keep the prize focused, accepting that it is arguable.
assessment.maturity: The theoretical idea is 40 years old and experimentally verified many times, and the 2022 prize to Aspect, Clauser and Zeilinger already recognised the entanglement experiments underlying quantum information. Recognition is timely but with overlap risk.
uncertainties: Whether Ekert should be included.
Ballot B027 is a similar candidate; I rank only this entry.
The practical security of real QKD devices (side channels) is still a topic of debate.
The 2022 prize may be taken to cover part of this ground.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: X-ray free-electron lasers are a new instrument that provides femtosecond, coherent, extremely bright X-ray pulses, opening time-resolved structural dynamics, single-shot imaging and nonlinear X-ray physics. This is a measurement-enabling invention of the type I value, with clear impact beyond physics in chemistry and structural biology.
assessment.attribution: Pellegrini contributed the SASE theory and long advocacy of the LCLS concept; Rossbach led the TESLA Test Facility/FLASH demonstration of SASE at short wavelengths; Ishikawa led SACLA. Others (Bonifacio, Kondratenko-Saldin, Madey, Emma at LCLS, Tschentscher at EuXFEL) have competing claims, so a fair configuration is hard.
assessment.maturity: Facilities have operated for 15 years with large user communities, so confirmation is excellent. The science output is mostly applications, which weakens the sense of one fundamental discovery.
uncertainties: Credit is spread over theory, accelerator engineering and facility building, and the supplied three may not be the decisive ones.
The Nobel physics tradition for instruments may be judged to favour the discoveries they enable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed vacuum injection beyond the standard quantum limit is now implemented in LIGO and Virgo, a direct and tangible case of quantum optics improving a flagship measurement. Caves's 1981 proposal, Kimble's first squeezed light generation (1986) and Schnabel's work on audio-band squeezing and GEO600 form a coherent chain from idea to instrument.
assessment.attribution: Caves gave the interferometer proposal, Slusher (not listed) and Kimble produced the first squeezed states, Schnabel and McKenzie/Lam and the GEO600 group developed the audio-band implementation. The credit list omits Slusher, Wu, Walls and Lam, so attribution is quite contested.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in operating gravitational-wave detectors, though its main impact is on a detector already recognised by the 2017 prize. Recognition is timely but possibly regarded as an incremental extension.
uncertainties: Many credible contributors (Slusher, Walls, Lam, McKenzie, Yuen) are not in the supplied names.
Whether the committee considers this an improvement of an already-recognised discovery rather than a new one.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ti:sapphire lasers and passive mode-locking (Kerr-lens and SESAM) made reliable, tunable femtosecond sources routine, which in turn underpinned frequency combs, attosecond science, multiphoton microscopy and ultrafast spectroscopy. The enabling impact on measurements throughout physics and chemistry is very large.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire laser (1982), Sibbett's group demonstrated Kerr-lens mode-locking (Spence, Kean, Sibbett 1991), and Keller invented the SESAM. The three roles are different and well separated, but Kerr-lens credit also involves Spence and Kean, who are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of independent use, so confirmation is not a concern. The question is whether the prize committee sees this as a laser-technology tool already well adjacent to the 2018 chirped pulse amplification prize and 2023 attosecond prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1999, 2005, 2018 and 2023 prizes in ultrafast science.
Credit for Kerr-lens mode-locking beyond Sibbett is unresolved.
